topic: Buying AI is NOT a strategy.

slides.hook: Buying **AI tools** is not an AI strategy

slides.title: You bought a tool, not a job
slides.body: Procurement teams sign AI contracts before anyone defines the work. Strategy starts with named tasks—support tickets, claims, reports—not with a vendor logo.

slides.title: No volume, no value
slides.body: AI pays off on repeat work. Prioritise tasks that happen weekly, burn real hours or cash, and have a clear “done” state. Everything else is a side project, not strategy.

slides.title: Impressed in demo, unclear in data
slides.body: Most AI pilots end with opinions, not evidence. Decide in advance which 2–3 numbers matter—time, cost, quality, satisfaction—and what “good” means in each.

slides.title: Risk is guessed, not governed
slides.body: Drafts and brainstorms are not the same as credit decisions or clinical notes. Classify use cases by impact, then set guardrails, approvals and monitoring that match the risk.

slides.title: Workflows stayed the same
slides.body: AI is bolted on at the edge of existing processes, so staff revert to old habits. Strategy-level adoption rewrites steps, roles and controls so AI is the default path, not an option.

slides.title: No owner, no change
slides.body: Tools arrive with no accountable lead. Effective programmes assign a single owner per use case—responsible for training, playbooks, metrics, risk and continuous improvement.

slides.title: What a real AI strategy buys
slides.body: You buy solved jobs, measurable outcomes, governed workflows and in-house capability. That means targeted use cases, clear KPIs, risk frameworks and teams trained to run them.

slides.line: Ready to move from AI purchases to AI performance?

caption:
